strengths: The Cartesian-3j construction in Eq. (5) provides a useful implementation bridge between spherical and Cartesian representations. Extending this construction to generalized coupling coefficients and Cartesian versions of three established architectures is a concrete engineering contribution.

The controlled 3BPA experiments cover NequIP, Allegro, and MACE across multiple truncations and report accuracy, runtime, memory, and parameter counts. They provide useful evidence that direct Cartesian implementations can retain similar predictive accuracy while incurring substantial computational costs.

The universal potential demonstrates practical usefulness: TACE-v1-OAM-M achieves F1 = 0.889 and thermal-conductivity error κSRME = 0.173 on Matbench Discovery. These results establish that the proposed implementation can support competitive large-scale materials modeling, even without leading the benchmark.

The manuscript explicitly acknowledges unfavorable high-rank scaling, missing fused kernels, and the absence of state-of-the-art performance. Appendix D supplies substantial universal-model training information, including hardware, optimizer settings, loss weights, and architecture. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: the second structural observation in Section 4.3 claims that components with the same output weight obtained using different contraction counts are linearly independent. After identifying their output representations, this conflicts with the multiplicity-one decomposition of two fixed irreducible inputs. For example, for symmetric traceless rank-2 tensors A and B, the scalar component of the single-contraction product is proportional to tr(AB), while the double contraction gives A:B—the same scalar. If independence instead refers to embeddings into different-rank ambient spaces, this must be defined and distinguished from independent equivariant couplings. Table 7 lists multiplicities but does not establish the claimed independence.

Soundness and presentation: the mathematical specification needs tighter treatment of representation conventions. Equation (6) assigns magnetic-index ranges to indices previously defined as Cartesian component indices. More substantively, the claimed O(3) framework does not explicitly track parity when mapping weight-ℓ components to rank-ℓ tensors; polar and axial representations require this distinction. These omissions impede verification of the advertised general construction.

Experimental support: the claimed importance of nonlinear interactions is not isolated. The linear universal model has two layers, whereas the selected gated model has five layers, so the κSRME improvement from 0.210 to 0.158 cannot be attributed specifically to gating. There are likewise no controlled ablations establishing the proposed contraction strategy, path restrictions, or delayed projection as 'best practices,' nor a matched spherical version of the final architecture supporting its claimed speed advantage.

Reliability of the controlled comparisons is insufficiently established. All 3BPA results use a single seed, despite appreciable differences in some extrapolation metrics. Tables 1–2 and Appendix Tables 5–6 also contain different Cartesian results under apparently identical configurations without clearly explaining the distinction: for example, the first cNequIP model has 300 K energy RMSE 6.5 versus 5.6. Numerical checks of transformed outputs, gradients, and equivariance would test implementation correctness more directly than independently trained prediction errors.

Originality and significance: Eq. (5) is a change of basis of an existing invariant coupling tensor, and Eq. (6) applies the established generalized-CG construction in that representation. The useful novelty therefore lies primarily in implementation and empirical understanding. Claims of establishing the theoretical foundations and current best-practice paradigm exceed the demonstrated advance over the cited ICTD, ICT-potential, and TACE work. Competitive leaderboard performance alone does not establish the benefit of the new framework over those alternatives.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful universal-model hyperparameter table. The supplied manuscript's code-availability section contains no usable locations; the 3BPA training recipe is not fully specified; and the MD speed benchmark omits the simulated system and timestep needed to interpret ps/day. The unexplained duplicate-table differences further obstruct reproduction. Together with the unresolved mathematical and experimental issues, these weaknesses prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Methodology: Equation (5) gives a principled construction of Cartesian coupling coefficients by transforming spherical couplings with the path matrices. Extending this construction to generalized couplings and an e3nn-style interface is a useful implementation contribution.

Significance: Comparing Cartesian versions of NequIP, Allegro, and MACE under matched architectural settings addresses a practical question. The reported memory and runtime measurements document the substantial cost of storing redundant Cartesian components, including out-of-memory cases.

Empirical value: TACE-v1-OAM-M provides a credible large-scale proof of concept. Its Matbench Discovery F1 of 0.889 and thermal-conductivity error of 0.173 are competitive with several established universal potentials, even though they do not establish superiority.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript has a clear overall progression and candidly discusses unfavorable scaling, missing optimized kernels, and the absence of state-of-the-art performance. Appendix D provides useful hardware and training details. The work uses established atomistic datasets, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—expressivity claims: Appendix E claims that highest-weight ICTP/ICTC supports all coupling paths and has exactly the same parameterization as general CG tensor products. As described, these operations omit antisymmetric channels: for two rank-1 vectors, highest-weight projection produces rank 2 and contraction produces rank 0, but neither produces the rank-1 cross-product channel. Additional antisymmetric operations or an explicit restriction of the claimed equivalence are needed. This objection concerns the proposed restricted architecture, not the basis-transformed coupling in Equation (5).

Soundness—mathematical specification: The framework repeatedly invokes O(3), but its representation labels and transformation discussion do not explicitly track parity or distinguish tensors from pseudotensors. This matters when identifying rank with angular weight. Moreover, the linear-independence statement across contraction orders in Section 4.3 needs a precise common-space definition: after mapping to the same output irrep, coupling two fixed irreps is multiplicity-free. Numerical observations through rank 4 do not resolve this ambiguity.

Evidence and presentation—unexplained discrepancies: Tables 1 and 5 report different Cartesian results for identically labeled configurations. For example, the first cNequIP configuration has 300 K energy RMSE 6.5 in Table 1 and 5.6 in Table 5. Tables 2 and 6 similarly disagree; the final cMACE configuration has dihedral energy RMSE 24.1 versus 19.0. Appendix A discusses an alternative construction, but the tables do not clearly identify whether these differences reflect that construction, normalization, or separate runs. The experimental record needs reconciliation.

Evidence—controlled comparison is insufficiently validated: Tables 1–2 explicitly use single runs, and some differences are substantial: the final MACE/cMACE configuration has 1200 K force RMSE 71.5/80.2 and dihedral energy RMSE 13.0/24.1. These results support broad feasibility but do not establish statistically comparable accuracy. For a claimed basis-only substitution, direct numerical checks of matched-weight outputs, forces, and equivariance would be more decisive than independently trained models; none are reported.

Significance and causal attribution: The nonlinearity conclusion is confounded by architectural changes. Section 5.3 describes the linear model as having two layers, whereas the selected gated model has five. The improvement from thermal-conductivity error 0.210 to 0.158 therefore does not isolate gating. Likewise, there is no matched spherical implementation of the final TACE architecture to substantiate its claimed Cartesian speed advantage, and Table 4 compares different architectures and execution backends. These omissions weaken the proposed 'best-practice' conclusions.

Originality: The main algebraic construction is a change of basis using previously developed path matrices, followed by the generalized-coupling construction already used in MACE. This can still provide useful new infrastructure and understanding, but the manuscript does not sufficiently distinguish its advance from the cited ICT decomposition work, TACE, and ICT potentials. Claims of establishing Cartesian theoretical foundations are broader than the demonstrated contribution.

Reproducibility: The supplied manuscript's Code Availability section contains blank repository locations. Although universal-model hyperparameters are provided, the controlled 3BPA experiments lack a complete training specification and reproducible configurations. The MD throughput benchmark also omits important workload details, including the simulated structure and timestep. Together with the unexplained table differences, these gaps prevent reliable reproduction of central results.

strengths: Significance: The framework provides a useful bridge between spherical and Cartesian implementations of equivariant MLIPs. Cartesian counterparts of NequIP, Allegro, and MACE make the practical consequences of changing representations easier to study.

Soundness: Equation (5) gives a natural change-of-basis construction of coupling coefficients. The experiments support the narrower conclusion that Cartesian implementations can achieve similar accuracy while suffering substantial memory and runtime costs at higher ranks.

Practical contribution: TACE-v1-OAM-M achieves competitive Matbench Discovery results, including F1 = 0.889 and thermal-conductivity error κSRME = 0.173. This is meaningful evidence that the proposed implementation can support large-scale atomistic modeling.

Presentation and limitations: The overall motivation is clear, and the discussion candidly acknowledges exponential storage growth, missing optimized kernels, and the absence of state-of-the-art performance. Appendix D supplies useful training and hardware details. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—contraction theory: Section 4.3 claims that, for fixed input weights and varying contraction order k, components with the same output weight are linearly independent. After mapping them into a common irreducible representation, this conflicts with the multiplicity-free decomposition of two SO(3) irreps: equivariant bilinear maps to a fixed output weight are proportional. For example, with two symmetric traceless rank-2 inputs, the scalar component of their single contraction and their double contraction are both proportional to their Frobenius inner product. If independence instead refers to embeddings in different ambient tensor spaces, the comparison needs a precise definition and does not establish independent coupling channels. This requires correction in a paper presenting a theoretical framework.

Presentation and evidential consistency: Tables 1–2 and Appendix Tables 5–6 report different Cartesian errors for apparently identical configurations without explaining the distinction. For example, the first cNequIP configuration has 300 K energy RMSE 6.5 in Table 1 versus 5.6 in Table 5; the last cMACE configuration has dihedral force RMSE 26.3 in Table 2 versus 22.4 in Table 6. If these correspond to different coupling constructions, that must be explicitly identified. Otherwise, the authoritative results are unclear.

Experimental support: The controlled comparisons cover one molecular dataset and explicitly omit multiple seeds. Some differences are substantial: Table 2 reports dihedral energy RMSE 13.0 versus 24.1 for the largest MACE/cMACE pair. Without variability estimates, these experiments cannot establish accuracy equivalence. Direct tests of mapped outputs, gradients, and equivariance would also provide stronger verification of the implementation than independently trained prediction errors.

Causal claims and significance: The proposed 'best-practice' recommendations are not supported by isolated ablations. The linear and nonlinear universal models differ in depth, so the improvement from κSRME 0.210 to 0.158 cannot be attributed specifically to gating. The claimed speed advantage over a spherical version of the proposed architecture is not accompanied by a matched benchmark; Table 4 compares different architectures and execution backends. Competitive leaderboard results establish feasibility but do not isolate the benefit of the proposed primitives or design choices.

Originality and technical precision: Equation (5) transforms existing coupling coefficients using previously established path matrices, and Equation (6) composes these transformed couplings. The strongest novelty appears to be implementation and empirical synthesis; the broader foundational claims need sharper differentiation from prior ICTD, ICT-potential, and TACE work. Appendix E also incorrectly characterizes Gaunt tensor products as introducing equivariance errors without qualification: restricting coupling paths affects expressivity, not inherently equivariance.

Reproducibility: The supplied Code Availability section contains no usable repository links. Although universal-model hyperparameters are provided, the 3BPA training configurations and numerical procedures supporting Table 7 are insufficiently specified for independent reproduction. Equation (6) also uses spherical-style magnetic-index ranges for Cartesian indices, leaving the generalized coupling definition ambiguous.
